Given how porous my bones are (so much so, that it is very difficult to detect hairline fractures on x-rays), what can I do to even slightly decrease my risk of new fractures at this point (either spontaneous fractures or from injuries)? I had a scare earlier when I was doing dishes and the whole part of the kitchen sink that the water comes out of detached itself and hit my hand. I am so grateful that I ended up with only a small bruise as it could easily have fractured my hand. In other words, no matter how careful I try to be, things just happen sometimes ...  Your expectation is reasonable. Bone loss after stopping Prolia is well documented, and bone density often drifts back toward where it was before treatment, so a result closer to 2021 than 2025 makes sense. (DEXA is also less precise in OI, so the trend matters more than any single number.) Please check these with your doctor, since I can't know what's safe for you. Medication: the biggest lever •	When Prolia is stopped, doctors often follow it with a bisphosphonate to slow the rebound loss. Humana suggested alendronate, but the pills can irritate the esophagus, which matters with your GERD and your tricky levothyroxine timing. It's worth asking whether a once-a-year IV version (zoledronic acid) would suit you better, or whether restarting Prolia at the $55.43 price makes more sense. Restarting is only worth it if you can stay on it without gaps. •	Ask whether your November 2 bloodwork can include vitamin D, calcium, and thyroid levels. Low vitamin D, or too much thyroid medication, can both weaken bone further. •	Ask whether your A1C of 6.2 on glimepiride is tighter than you need. I'm sorry you've been dealing with bad stomach aches for the past few weeks. ❤️ I wouldn't recommend simply waiting it out at this point, especially if the pain has been significant or keeps coming back.  My recommendation is to arrange a medical appointment as soon as possible, ideally today or within the next day or two. Stomach pain that persists for several weeks deserves medical evaluation, even if it comes and goes.  1. Should you see a doctor or a specialist? I'd suggest starting with one of these options:  Primary care doctor: A good starting point if you have one. They can examine you, evaluate possible causes, and determine whether you need further testing. Gastroenterologist: This is a specialist who treats problems involving the digestive system, including the stomach, intestines, and esophagus. Given that your symptoms have lasted several weeks, seeing one may be appropriate. Urgent care: Consider this if you cannot get a timely appointment with your regular doctor and the pain is ongoing or getting worse. Some conditions require an emergency department rather than urgent care. You don't necessarily need to see a specialist first. A primary care doctor can help determine which type of evaluation you need.  2. When should you seek emergency care? Please don't wait for a routine appointment if you experience any of the following:  Severe or rapidly worsening abdominal pain. A very swollen, hard, or extremely tender abdomen. Vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds. Bloody stools or black, tarry stools. Persistent vomiting that prevents you from keeping fluids down. Fainting, confusion, or difficulty breathing. Abdominal pain accompanied by chest pain. These symptoms can indicate a potentially serious problem that needs immediate evaluation.   3. Can you tell what might be causing the stomach aches? There are many possible causes, including indigestion, constipation, inflammation of the stomach lining, ulcers, and other digestive conditions. The location of your pain and the symptoms accompanying it can help a doctor narrow down the possibilities. convo_text: what diabetes  Diabetes mellitus is a chronic (long-lasting) health condition that affects how your body turns food into energy.  Most of the food you eat is broken down into glucose (sugar), which is released into your bloodstream. When your blood sugar goes up, it signals your pancreas to release insulin. Insulin acts like a key to let blood sugar into your body's cells for use as energy.  If you have diabetes, your body either doesn't make enough insulin or can't effectively use the insulin it does make. This causes sugar to build up in your bloodstream, leading to high blood sugar levels. Over time, high blood sugar can cause health complications such as heart disease, vision loss, and kidney damage.  Main Types of Diabetes Type 1 Diabetes: An autoimmune condition where the body attacks and destroys the cells in the pancreas that make insulin. People with type 1 diabetes produce little to no insulin and must take daily insulin injections to survive. It is usually diagnosed in children and young adults, though it can develop at any age.  Type 2 Diabetes: A condition where the body either doesn't produce enough insulin or resists insulin (insulin resistance). This is the most common form of diabetes, often linked to factors such as genetics, lifestyle, and weight, and it typically develops in adults, though it is increasingly seen in younger people.  Gestational Diabetes: A type of diabetes that develops in some women during pregnancy. It usually goes away after the baby is born, but it increases the person's risk of developing type 2 diabetes later in life.  Common Symptoms When blood sugar is high, common signs can include:  Frequent urination (especially at night)  Excessive thirst  Unexplained weight loss  Extreme fatigue or tiredness  Blurred vision  Slow-healing sores or frequent infections  what age does it affect the most  The age group most affected by diabetes depends significantly on the specific type of diabetes:  Type 2 Diabetes (Most Common Type) Type 2 diabetes makes up roughly 90% to 95% of all diabetes cases and most commonly affects adults aged 45 to 64, closely followed by adults aged 65 and older.  Highest Prevalence: Adults 65 and older have the highest percentage rate of diabetes (about 25% to 30% of seniors have diagnosed diabetes).  Most New Diagnoses: The greatest number of new cases each year occurs among adults between aged 45 and 64.  Changing Trends: While it historically affected older adults, type 2 diabetes is increasingly being diagnosed in young adults, teens, and children due to rising rates of obesity and sedentary lifestyles.  Type 1 Diabetes Type 1 diabetes accounts for about 5% to 10% of cases and is most frequently diagnosed in children, teens, and young adults (typically between ages 4 and 14), though it can develop at any age.  Gestational Diabetes Gestational diabetes occurs only during pregnancy, usually developing between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. It is most common in pregnant women aged 35 and older.  Are you asking out of general curiosity, or are you concerned about yourself or a family member?

convo_text: Can an allergic reaction appear slowly  Yes, allergic reactions can definitely appear slowly. While many people associate allergies with immediate "anaphylactic" reactions that happen within minutes, others can take hours or even days to manifest.  Medical professionals generally categorize these reactions based on how quickly they develop:  1. Immediate-Onset Reactions (Minutes to Hours) These are typically IgE-mediated reactions. Symptoms usually appear within seconds to two hours after exposure.  Examples: Hives, swelling, or hay fever.  Common Triggers: Peanuts, bee stings, or pollen.  2. Delayed-Onset Reactions (Hours to Days) These are often Non-IgE-mediated or T-cell mediated reactions. The immune system takes longer to mobilize, so you might not notice anything for quite a while.  Contact Dermatitis: This is a classic slow reaction. If you touch poison ivy or a certain type of metal (like nickel), the itchy rash might not appear for 24 to 72 hours.  Drug Hypersensitivity: Some medication rashes (like those from penicillin or sulfa drugs) can take several days or even a week of consistent use before they show up.  Food Protein-Induced Enterocolitis Syndrome (FPIES): Unlike a typical food allergy, this gastrointestinal reaction usually happens 2 to 6 hours after eating the trigger food.  3. Biphasic Reactions In some cases, a person might have an immediate reaction that seems to go away, only for a "second wave" of symptoms to return several hours later without any new exposure to the allergen.  Note: If you are experiencing difficulty breathing, swelling of the tongue or throat, or a rapid drop in blood pressure, seek emergency medical attention immediately, as these are signs of a severe reaction regardless of how quickly they started. Distinguishing between a standard side effect and a true allergic reaction is important for deciding whether to continue the medication.  Here is how to tell the difference:  1. Common Symptoms of an Allergic Reaction Allergic reactions involve your immune system and typically present through the skin or respiratory system.  Symptom Type	What to Look For Hives (Urticaria)	Raised, red, extremely itchy welts. These often appear quickly and can "migrate" to different parts of the body. Maculopapular Rash	Flat red patches and small bumps. This is common with antibiotics like amoxicillin and often appears 24 to 72 hours after the first dose. Swelling (Angioedema)	Noticeable puffiness in the face, lips, tongue, or around the eyes. Respiratory Issues	Sudden wheezing, a persistent cough, or a feeling of "tightness" in the throat or chest. 2. Allergy vs. Common Side Effects Many people mistake "undesirable effects" for allergies. Side effects are common and usually don't require stopping the medication unless they are severe.  Side Effects (Non-Allergic): Nausea, mild stomach cramps, diarrhea, or a headache. These are caused by the drug's effect on your body (or your gut bacteria) rather than an immune response.  Allergic Reaction: Itching, rashes, swelling, or breathing trouble.  3. The "Red Flags" (Seek Immediate Help) If you notice any of the following, stop taking the medication and go to an urgent care or emergency room immediately:  Difficulty breathing or swallowing.  Blistering or peeling of the skin, or sores inside the mouth/eyes.  A high fever accompanied by a spreading rash.  Fainting or extreme dizziness (signs of a drop in blood pressure). What did I catch? --- Those symptoms — sudden onset fatigue, body aches, fever (feeling hot followed by chills), and nasal congestion — point strongly to influenza (the flu). The key tell is the sudden onset and the fever/chills cycle, which is classic flu behavior.  A few possibilities in rough order of likelihood:  Influenza is the top candidate. Flu hits fast (often within hours), and body aches + fever + chills is its signature combination. Congestion is common too.  COVID-19 is also worth considering — it can present nearly identically, including the fatigue, aches, and fever. Worth taking a home test if you have one.  A common cold usually comes on more gradually and rarely causes significant fever or body aches, so the sudden onset makes this less likely — though not impossible.  A few things to do now:  Rest and hydrate aggressively Take a COVID test to rule it out OTC options like acetaminophen or ibuprofen can help with the fever and aches If it is flu, antiviral medications like Tamiflu are most effective within the first 48 hours — so if symptoms worsen, see a doctor soon  Hope you feel better quickly, [NAME REDACTED]. Lots of fluids and rest.  Note: I'm not a doctor — if you develop difficulty breathing, a very high fever, or symptoms that worsen rapidly, seek medical attention. --- How long does the flu last --- For most healthy adults, the flu runs 5–7 days, though you may feel wiped out for up to 2 weeks.  The rough timeline:  Days 1–2 — Peak misery. Fever, chills, aches, fatigue hit hardest. Days 3–4 — Fever usually breaks. Congestion and cough may worsen as the body clears things out. Days 5–7 — Most symptoms resolve for healthy adults. Week 2 — Lingering fatigue and cough are normal and can drag on even after you otherwise feel fine.  A few things that can extend it: not resting enough early on, secondary infections (like a sinus infection or bronchitis developing on top), or if you're immunocompromised.  The fatigue in particular has a way of sticking around longer than you'd expect — don't be surprised if you feel worn down for a full week after the acute phase. --- I'm feeling a bit better today, no aches or chills. Sore throat, no runny nose. Still think it's the flu? --- That progression actually makes the flu a bit less likely. Here's why:  The flu's hallmark — the severe body aches, chills, and fever — typically persists for several days. convo_text: Dealing with knee pain after challenging travel with lots of walking and stair climbing, what can i do to alleviate knee pain and get back to normal? Dealing with knee pain after a trip filled with heavy walking and stair climbing is very common, especially when your joints undergo more repeated impact and stress than usual. ​Here are practical, step-by-step strategies to help ease the discomfort, calm down inflammation, and get your knees feeling back to normal: ​1. Immediate Care: Rest & Calming Inflammation ​In the first few days post-travel, focus on giving the joint tissue a chance to rest and heal: ​Relative Rest: Avoid high-impact activities, running, or extra stair climbing for a few days. You don't need to stay completely still, but avoid pushing through sharp or increasing pain. ​Ice Therapy: Apply an ice pack wrapped in a thin towel to the affected knee(s) for 15–20 minutes, 2 to 3 times a day. Ice helps numb sharp ache and reduce localized inflammation. ​Targeted Elevation: When resting, relaxing, or sitting back, prop your leg up on a couple of pillows so your knee is elevated at or above heart level to assist with joint drainage. ​Over-the-Counter Relief: Short-term use of anti-inflammatory medications (like ibuprofen or naproxen) or topical gels (such as Voltaren/diclofenac) can help manage pain and swelling. (Be sure to check with your pharmacist or doctor if you take other medications or have underlying health considerations.) ​2. Gentle Motion & Soft Tissue Relief ​Once the initial sharp discomfort subsides, gentle movement helps flush out fluid build-up and prevents stiffness from setting in: ​Low-Impact Movement: Gentle, flat-surface walking or light stationary cycling with low resistance promotes blood flow without straining the knee joint. ​Gentle Calf & Hamstring Stretches: Tight hamstrings and calves put extra tension on the knee cap and joint capsule. Perform soft, static stretches for your hamstrings and calves—hold each stretch gently for 20–30 seconds without bouncing. ​Foam Rolling or Massage: Gently massage or use a foam roller on your quads (front of the thigh) and calves to release tight muscle knots that pull on the knee. Avoid rolling directly over the knee bone or joint itself. ​3. Gradual Return to Routine ​Pace Your Activities: As your knee starts feeling better, gradually ramp your daily walking distances back up rather than jumping straight into full intensity. ​Mindful Footwear: Stick to supportive, well-cushioned shoes with good arch support while your knees are recovering. Avoid flat, unsupportive shoes or hard soles. ​⚠️ When to See a Doctor ​While post-travel overuse pain usually settles with a few days of self-care, reach out to a healthcare professional or primary care doctor if you experience any of the following: ​Inability to bear weight on the leg or walk a few steps. ​Significant, visible knee swelling, heat, or redness. ​A feeling that the knee is "locking," catching, or giving out underneath you. ​Pain that persists or worsens after 1 to 2 weeks of conservative care. ​How is the knee feeling right now—is it more of a dull ache around the kneecap, or is there stiffness and swelling in a specific spot? Dull ache, feel weak when trying to stand up from sitting. That specific sensation—a dull ache combined with weakness or fatigue in the front of the knee when trying to stand up from a seated position—is classic patellofemoral stress or mild tendon strain. ​When you do a lot of walking and stair climbing (especially descending stairs, which acts like a heavy braking motion for your quads), your quadriceps muscles and the tendon supporting your kneecap work overtime. When they get overloaded, the kneecap tracks slightly differently, making the act of pushing up from a chair feel weak, heavy, or achy. ​To help your knees recover and regain their strength for standing up, you can add a few targeted, low-load techniques: ​1. Support the Sit-to-Stand Motion ​Use Your Hands: For the next few days, don't hesitate to push off the arms of the chair or use your hands on your thighs to take some of the load off your knees as you stand up. ​Mind Your Form: When rising from a chair, scoot slightly forward, keep your weight centered over your mid-foot, and lean your torso forward just a bit before pushing up. This distributes the work more evenly between your glutes, hips, and thighs instead of dumping all the pressure straight onto your knees. ​2. Gentle Quad Activation (Without Deep Bending) ​Since the weakness is tied to your quads, waking them up gently without bending the knee under heavy load can help restore that stable feeling: ​Seated Quad Sets: ​Sit on a chair with your legs bent at 90 degrees. ​Slowly straighten one leg out in front of you, flexing your foot so your toes point toward the ceiling. ​Squeeze the muscle on the front of your thigh (your quad) hard for 5 seconds. ​Lower it back down with control. Repeat 10 times per leg. This reactivates the muscle without requiring your knee to bear body weight. ​Seated Heel Slides: ​Sit on a chair or the edge of a bed with your feet flat. ​Slowly slide your heel forward as far as is comfortable, then pull it back under the chair. ​This helps lubricate the joint and ease stiffness without strain. ​3. Continue Managing the Load ​Keep Ice Handy: If the dull ache flares up after sitting for a while or at the end of the day, a 15-minute ice pack application can calm down any mild inflammation in the tendon. ​Avoid Deep Squats: For the next few days, steer clear of deep squats, lunges, or heavy stair climbing until that weakness when standing up starts to fade. ​How are your quads feeling overall—are they feeling tight or fatigued to the touch as well? I want to learn which foods are high in protein and other important nutrients, how much protein I should aim to eat daily, and how to incorporate more fruits, vegetables, healthy fats, and fiber into my meals. I am also looking for affordable food options because I am a graduate student on a budget, so I need meals that are simple to prepare and fit into my busy schedule. I enjoy variety and do not want to eat the same meals every day, and I am not a fan of overnight oats. Please recommend specific foods, explain their nutritional benefits, and suggest easy breakfast, lunch, dinner, and snack ideas that support my goals. Carbohydrates  Rice, potatoes, oats, fruit and whole grains.  Provide energy for workouts and everyday activities.  Healthy fats  Nuts, seeds, olive oil, avocado and fatty fish.  Support hormone function and help absorb vitamins.  Fiber and produce  Aim for roughly 25 g or more of fiber daily.  Support digestion, fullness and heart health.  One easy approach is to spread your protein across the day rather than trying to eat most of it at dinner.  Meal	Example protein target Breakfast	25–30 g Lunch	25–35 g Dinner	30–35 g Snacks	20–30 g total  These are flexible targets, not strict rules. You can adjust portions according to hunger, activity and your schedule.  Important for your goals: You cannot specifically burn fat from your belly through food or abdominal exercises alone. Overall fat loss, if needed, happens throughout the body, while strength training and sufficient nutrition help you build muscle, including your glutes. Avoid aggressive calorie restriction because it can interfere with muscle growth and recovery.  2. Best affordable foods for your fitness goals  You don't need expensive protein powders, specialty health foods, or prepackaged fitness meals. Many everyday foods provide the nutrients your body needs.  Chicken, turkey and lean ground meat  25–30 g protein  Approximate protein per 3–4 oz cooked serving, depending on the meat.  Excellent for muscle repair and growth. Buy family packs when affordable, divide into portions and freeze. Ground turkey and chicken thighs can also be budget-friendly. Combine eggs with Greek yogurt or beans when you need more protein.  Plain Greek yogurt and cottage cheese  15–23 g protein  Per roughly ¾–1 cup, depending on product. Salmon and sardines can also provide omega-3 fats. Rotate tuna with other fish and protein sources rather than relying on tuna daily. Greek yogurt parfait  Greek yogurt, banana or berries, a small amount of granola and chia seeds.  20–25 g protein  No cooking required. Use frozen fruit to save money.  3. Breakfast wrap  Scrambled eggs, black beans, spinach and a little cheese in a tortilla.  18–25 g protein  Make two at once and refrigerate one for a busy morning.  4. Banana peanut butter smoothie  Milk, Greek yogurt, banana, peanut butter and ice.  20–30 g protein  Great when you need breakfast on the way to class or work.  Lunch  1. Chicken rice bowl  Chicken, rice, broccoli or mixed vegetables, and your favorite seasoning or sauce.  30–40 g protein  Change the flavor with jerk seasoning, garlic and herbs, salsa or a lemon dressing.  2. Tuna sandwich or wrap  Tuna mixed with Greek yogurt or a little mayonnaise, plus lettuce, tomato and whole-grain bread or a wrap.  25–35 g protein  Serve with fruit or carrots for extra fiber and nutrients.  3. Chicken and black bean burrito bowl  Chicken, black beans, rice, corn, tomatoes and a little avocado.  30–40 g protein  Beans stretch your meat portions and provide extra fiber.  4. Lentil soup and toast  Lentils, carrots, onion, canned tomatoes and broth, served with whole-grain toast.  15–22 g protein  Make a large pot and freeze portions. Add chicken or a boiled egg if desired.  Dinner  1. Caribbean-style chicken dinner  Jerk or herb-seasoned chicken, rice and peas, and steamed cabbage.  30–40 g protein  You can keep familiar Caribbean foods in your diet. Adjust portions to your hunger and activity.  2. Salmon, potatoes and broccoli  Baked salmon, roasted potatoes and broccoli with olive oil and seasoning.  25–35 g protein  Use frozen salmon fillets or substitute canned salmon if cheaper.  3. Boiled eggs and whole-grain crackers  About 12–15 g protein.  Roasted chickpeas  Protein, fiber and a crunchy alternative to chips. The protein total can vary with brands and portion sizes. You may need additional meals or snacks to meet your energy needs, particularly on demanding workout days.  5. Grocery shopping on a graduate-student budget  A good strategy is to build your grocery list around a few inexpensive proteins, flexible carbohydrates and produce options, then change the seasonings and combinations.  Buy these protein staples  * Eggs and store-brand plain Greek yogurt * Chicken thighs or chicken breast on sale * Canned tuna, salmon or sardines * Canned beans, dried lentils and chickpeas * Cottage cheese or milk when affordable * Ground turkey or tofu when on sale  Choose inexpensive meal bases  * Rice, oats and potatoes * Whole-wheat pasta and bread * Tortillas and beans * Peanut butter and unsalted nuts  Save on fruits and vegetables  * Frozen broccoli, spinach and mixed vegetables * Frozen berries instead of fresh berries when cheaper * Bananas, apples, oranges and seasonal fruit * Carrots, cabbage and onions * Canned tomatoes and low-sodium vegetables  Smart substitutions  If a recipe calls for…	Try this instead Fresh berries	Frozen berries or seasonal fruit Fresh salmon	Canned salmon or another affordable fish Chicken breast	Chicken thighs or sale-priced turkey Quinoa	Rice, potatoes or whole-wheat pasta Protein bars	Greek yogurt, eggs or cottage cheese Bagged salad	Cabbage, carrots or whole lettuce Fresh vegetables	Frozen mixed vegetables Expensive salad dressings	Olive oil, lemon, vinegar and seasoning  Practical ways to spend less  * Plan around sales. Choose two or three proteins for the week rather than buying everything. * Reuse ingredients differently. Chicken can become a rice bowl one day, a wrap the next, and a salad topping later. * Cook once, eat more than once. Prepare a batch of rice, a protein and vegetables, then refrigerate or freeze individual portions. * Use store brands. Compare the price per ounce rather than just the package price. * Avoid paying extra for marketing. Foods labeled fitness, high protein or fat burning are not automatically better. * Check canned food labels. Lower-sodium options can be helpful; draining and rinsing beans can reduce some sodium.  Affordable protein and fiber staples such as eggs, beans, lentils, yogurt, oats and frozen produce are practical foundations for a nutritious diet. Verywell Health +1  6. How to eat for glute growth and reduce belly fat sustainably  Pair nutrition with progressive strength training.  Train your glutes consistently, gradually increasing resistance or repetitions as your strength improves. Hip thrusts, squats, Romanian deadlifts, lunges and glute bridges can all help. Nutrition supports the process, but training provides the stimulus for muscle growth.  Don't cut out carbohydrates.  Rice, potatoes, oats and fruit provide useful workout fuel. You can build a balanced plate with protein, carbohydrates, vegetables and some healthy fat.  Drink water and prioritize recovery.  Keep water with you during classes and work. Eat regularly enough to support training, and aim for 7–9 hours of sleep when possible.  Aim for consistency, not perfection.  You can still enjoy Caribbean dishes, restaurant meals, desserts and snacks. Focus on what you do most of the time instead of labeling foods as good or bad.  For fiber, work toward roughly 25–28 grams per day through fruit, vegetables, whole grains, beans and seeds. Increase your intake gradually and drink enough water to help avoid digestive discomfort. The FDA lists 28 grams as the Daily Value for fiber on food labels. FDA +1  Since you want to build your glutes while also changing your body composition, avoid crash diets. If fat loss is appropriate for you, a modest energy deficit may help, but eating enough to support muscle growth and recovery is important too. You can also improve strength and body composition without the scale dropping substantially.  7. Your simple weekly food-prep routine  You don't have to meal prep every single meal on Sunday. Try this flexible routine instead:  * Pick three proteins: for example, chicken, eggs and beans, with Greek yogurt for snacks. * Prepare two carbohydrates: rice and roasted potatoes, or rice and pasta. * Choose three vegetables and two fruits: include frozen options to make your food last longer. * Cook two main dishes: one for the first part of the week and one for later in the week. * Keep backup meals available: eggs on toast, tuna wraps, yogurt bowls or beans and rice for nights when you're too busy to cook.  Refrigerate cooked leftovers promptly and generally use them within 3–4 days, freezing extra portions if needed.  The bottom line: you don't need a perfect diet or an expensive grocery bill to make progress. Build meals around affordable protein, add fiber-rich foods, eat enough to fuel your workouts, and rotate flavors so your plan remains enjoyable.

convo_text: My son started taking gaunfacine about a month ago and four days ago, upped the dose to 2mg. Ive noticed while he falls asleep easier and faster, he's been waking a lot in the night and he never used to do that. 1. Is that typical of the medicine or could it be related to the fact that he no longer takes melatonin? And 2. If it is the meds, would switching to giving it to him in the morning help instead of taking it at night?  What you're describing is possible with guanfacine, but it's not the most classic effect.  A few thoughts:  1. Could it be the guanfacine? Yes. Guanfacine often helps children fall asleep more easily because it can cause drowsiness, especially when the dose is increased. However, some children experience changes in their sleep pattern as their body adjusts, including:  More nighttime awakenings Lighter sleep More vivid dreams Restless sleep Since the increased waking started about 4 days after increasing to 2 mg, the timing does make the medication a reasonable suspect.  2. Could it be from stopping melatonin? Absolutely.  Melatonin is more than just a "fall asleep" supplement. It also helps regulate the body's sleep-wake cycle. Some children will:  Continue falling asleep fine after stopping it But have trouble staying asleep Wake earlier than usual Wake multiple times overnight Given that he is still falling asleep quickly but is waking repeatedly, the loss of melatonin's effect on sleep maintenance could fit what you're seeing.  3. Would switching guanfacine to the morning help? Maybe, but I would not change the timing without checking with his prescriber first.  The answer depends on:  Whether he's taking immediate-release or extended-release guanfacine Why he was prescribed it (ADHD, emotional regulation, etc.) How sleepy it makes him during the day If the medication is contributing to the nighttime waking, a morning dose might help. On the other hand, if it makes him sleepy, moving it to the morning could cause daytime fatigue and not necessarily fix the sleep issue.  What I would watch for Since the dose increase was only 4 days ago, I'd consider:  Tracking wake-ups for the next 1-2 weeks Noting what time he wakes Noting whether he seems fully awake or just briefly stirs Looking for other changes from the dose increase (more tired, irritable, emotional, dizzy, headaches) Many medication-related sleep changes improve as the body adjusts over the first couple of weeks after a dose increase.  My guess Based on the timing alone, I wouldn't be surprised if it's either:  His body adjusting to the increase to 2 mg, or The fact that melatonin was stopped at about the same time. Did he stop the melatonin when the guanfacine was increased to 2 mg, or had he already been off the melatonin for a while before the dose change? That timing would help narrow down which is more likely.       If its from the medicine, is that something that typically goes away as their body gets used to it Yes, if the nighttime waking is being caused by the guanfacine itself, there's a decent chance it will improve as his body adjusts.  With guanfacine, many side effects are most noticeable:  When first starting the medication For a week or two after a dose increase Then they often lessen over the next couple of weeks.  That said, every child is different. The most common adjustment effect is usually sleepiness/tiredness, but sleep disruptions can occur for some kids. If the waking started right after the increase to 2 mg, I'd personally be inclined to give it a little more time (assuming his prescriber hasn't advised otherwise and he isn't having other concerning symptoms).  A few questions that can help distinguish what's happening:  When he wakes up, is he able to go back to sleep fairly quickly? Is he waking once or twice, or is it happening repeatedly throughout the night? Does he seem more rested, less rested, or about the same during the day? How long ago was the melatonin stopped relative to the dose increase? One thing I would not do without talking to his doctor is immediately switch the dose to morning. If the medication is making him sleepy and helping him fall asleep, moving it could trade nighttime waking for daytime fatigue.  If the awakenings continue beyond 1-2 weeks after the increase, are getting worse, or he's becoming exhausted during the day, that's usually a good time to check in with the prescriber. They can advise whether to:  Continue and wait for adjustment, Change the timing, Adjust the dose, or Reintroduce a sleep aid if appropriate. Out of curiosity, how old is your son, and is he taking the extended-release guanfacine (Intuniv) or the immediate-release version? That makes a difference in how dosing time is usually handled.

convo_text: What if hand foot and mouth isn't treated  Hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) is a viral illness that is typically self-limiting, meaning most people get completely better on their own within 7 to 10 days without any medical treatment. Because it is caused by a virus (usually coxsackievirus), antibiotics will not cure it.    Instead of treating the virus itself, medical care focuses entirely on managing symptoms. If left without supportive care, or in rare instances, the progression can lead to specific concerns:  1. Dehydration (The Most Common Risk)  The most frequent and significant complication of HFMD isn't the virus itself, but the pain it causes. Because the mouth and throat sores can make swallowing extremely painful, children (and occasionally adults) may refuse to eat or drink.     The risk: If fluid intake drops too low, dehydration can occur quickly, particularly in toddlers and young children. Severe dehydration may require a hospital visit for intravenous (IV) fluids.     Management: Encouraging cold liquids, popsicles, or smoothies can help soothe the throat while keeping fluid levels up. Over-the-counter pain relievers like ibuprofen or acetaminophen can also reduce throat pain enough to allow drinking.    2. Prolonged Discomfort  Without pain management, the fever, throat soreness, and overall malaise will simply have to run their course. While the body's immune system will naturally fight off the infection, letting it go completely unmanaged can mean several days of high fussiness, poor sleep, and sore hands and feet.    3. Rare Complications  While exceedingly rare, certain strains of the viruses that cause HFMD can lead to more serious medical issues that require immediate professional intervention:     Viral (Aseptic) Meningitis: A rare infection and inflammation of the membranes covering the brain and spinal cord, causing high fever, severe headache, and a stiff neck.     Encephalitis: An even rarer, potentially life-threatening inflammation of the brain itself.     Nail Shedding: Weeks after recovering, a small number of children experience temporary shedding of a fingernail or toenail, which typically regrows entirely on its own.     Monitor for red flags: Contact a healthcare provider immediately if you or your child show signs of dehydration (such as crying without tears or no wet diapers for 8+ hours), a fever lasting more than 3 days, a stiff neck, extreme lethargy, or symptoms that worsen after a week.

convo_text: Conversation with Gemini Why is the top of my foot hurting  Pain on the top of the foot (the dorsal surface) is quite common and can stem from several different structures, including bones, tendons, nerves, or joints.  Common Causes of Top-of-Foot Pain Extensor Tendonitis  What it is: Inflammation of the tendons that pull your toes up toward your leg.  Common symptoms: A aching or burning pain across the top of the foot, often worsened by flexing your foot upward or running/walking. It is frequently caused by wearing shoes that are tied too tightly or tight calf muscles.  Stress Fracture  What it is: A tiny crack in one of the metatarsal bones (the long bones leading to your toes).  Common symptoms: Pinpointed pain on a specific bone that gradually gets worse with weight-bearing activities, accompanied by localized swelling or tenderness to the touch.  Midfoot Osteoarthritis or Bone Spurs  What it is: Wear-and-tear of the cartilage in the tarsometatarsal joints, or extra bone growth on top of the midfoot joints (sometimes called a "midfoot boss").  Common symptoms: A firm bump on top of the arch area, stiffness in the foot (especially in the morning), and pain when walking or pressing on the area.  Nerve Entrapment or Irritation  What it is: Compression of the superficial peroneal nerve or deep peroneal nerve on the top of the foot.  Common symptoms: Burning, tingling, numbness, or a shooting sensation traveling down toward the toes. This is often caused by tight footwear or direct pressure.  Lisfranc (Midfoot) Injury  What it is: Sprain, dislocation, or fracture of the ligament and bones in the midfoot region.  Common symptoms: Pain, swelling, and potential bruising on the top or bottom of the foot, usually following a specific twist, fall, or impact.  Helpful Questions to Narrow It Down To help narrow down what might be going on, could you share a bit more context?  Did it start suddenly (after a specific twist, stub, or fall) or build up gradually over days or weeks?  Is there visible swelling, redness, bruising, or a hard bump on top of your foot?  What does the pain feel like (e.g., sharp, dull/aching, burning, tingling, or throbbing)?  Does anything make it better or worse (e.g., untying your shoes, walking, flexing your toes, resting)?  Self-Care & When to See a Doctor Initial Rest & Relief: If there's no severe injury, resting the foot, applying ice wrapped in a towel for 15–20 minutes at a time, loosening your shoe laces, and avoiding hard impact can help reduce strain.  When to seek prompt medical care: Seek care right away if you cannot put any weight on your foot, if there is visible deformity, severe sudden swelling or bruising, numbness/loss of feeling in your toes, or signs of infection (red streaks, warmth, fever).  This is for informational purposes only. For medical advice or diagnosis, consult a professional. There is no swelling but I do run daily  Since you run daily and don't have any swelling, that narrows down the possibilities significantly. Repetitive impact combined with daily training makes running-related overuse injuries the most likely culprits.  Top Likely Causes for Daily Runners Extensor Tendonitis (Most Common)  Why it fits: The extensor tendons run along the top of the foot to lift your toes. Repetitive running—especially uphill, on uneven surfaces, or with laces tied too tightly over the dorsum of the foot—can irritate these tendons without necessarily causing noticeable swelling right away.  Key sign: Pain when pulling your toes or foot upward against gentle resistance, or pain when pressing directly on the tendons along the top of the foot.  Early Metatarsal Stress Reaction  Why it fits: Before a full stress fracture develops (which usually causes localized swelling and sharp pain), repetitive pounding can cause a "stress reaction" (bone inflammation).  Key sign: A deep, aching pain over one of the long midfoot bones that gets noticeably worse toward the end of a run or when bearing weight, and improves with rest.  Nerve Compression ("Lace Bite")  Why it fits: Tight shoelaces, rigid shoe tongues, or wearing high-mileage running shoes that have lost structural support can compress the superficial nerve running across the top of your foot.  Key sign: Burning, tingling, or pain that feels close to the skin surface and improves immediately when taking off your shoes.  Navicular Stress Reaction or Midfoot Joint Irritation  Why it fits: If the pain is closer to the high arch/ankle junction on top of the foot, the repetitive force of foot strikes can irritate the midfoot joints or the navicular bone.  Immediate Action Steps for Runners Check Your Lacing: Try a window-lacing (or parallel-lacing) technique to skip the eyelets directly over the painful area, taking pressure off the top of the foot.  Inspect Your Shoes: Check the mileage on your current running shoes. Shoes that are worn out lose shock absorption, transferring extra impact force directly into the midfoot bones and tendons.  Calf & Achilles Mobility: Tight calves increase stress on the top-of-foot tendons during the push-off phase of your stride. Gentle calf stretching (gastrocnemius and soleus) can relieve tension.  Temporarily Adjust Volume: Swap high-impact daily runs for low-impact cross-training (like cycling or swimming) for a few days to see if resting the repetitive impact resolves the aching.  What to Watch For Does the pain feel like a surface muscle/tendon ache when pulling your toes up, or is it a deep bone pain localized to one precise spot when you press on it? Knowing if it worsens at a specific point in your stride can also help pinpoint the cause.  This is for informational purposes only. For medical advice or diagnosis, consult a professional.

convo_text: Percentage of people need to get 2nd eye's cataract surgery after doing the first one. Is it a must?  No, it is **not automatically a must** to have cataract surgery on the second eye after the first eye is done. However, many people eventually choose to do both eyes.  ### How often do people have the second eye done? Studies and real-world data generally show that **70–90% of patients** who undergo cataract surgery in one eye eventually have surgery in the other eye as well. The exact percentage depends on age, health, and how much cataract is present in the second eye.  ### Reasons people proceed with the second eye - Cataracts are usually an **age-related process affecting both eyes**, although one eye may be worse initially. - Better **depth perception** and **binocular vision** when both eyes see similarly. - Reduced imbalance if one eye has an artificial lens and the other still has a cataract. - Better night driving and overall visual quality.  ### Reasons some people do not - The second eye has only a mild cataract and vision remains good. - The patient is satisfied with their vision after the first surgery. - Other eye diseases limit the potential benefit. - Medical or personal reasons make surgery undesirable.  ### Is there a downside to leaving the second eye untreated? Sometimes, yes. After surgery in one eye, you may notice: - A large prescription difference between the eyes (**anisometropia**) - Difficulty with depth perception - Trouble adapting to glasses - More glare or blur from the cataract eye  But if the second eye still sees well (for example 20/25 or 20/30) and doesn't bother you, many ophthalmologists simply monitor it until symptoms develop.  ### Typical timing When both eyes need surgery, the second eye is often done: - **1–4 weeks later** in the U.S. - Sometimes even sooner depending on the surgeon and circumstances.  ### For premium lenses Since you've recently been asking about the Johnson & Johnson Odyssey lens, this is particularly relevant. Multifocal and extended-depth-of-focus lenses such as Johnson & Johnson TECNIS Odyssey IOL generally work best when implanted in **both eyes**, because the brain can better combine the images from two similar lenses. Many patients who choose an Odyssey lens in the first eye eventually decide to have the second eye done as well if a cataract is present.  If you're considering Odyssey for one eye, I can also explain the pros and cons of: 1. Odyssey in one eye only, 2. Odyssey in both eyes, 3. Odyssey + monofocal mix-and-match approaches.

convo_text: What does it mean if I have eczema dry spots on my skin but they are only there for a few days or weeks and then randomly disappear for a period of time? If you have dry, eczema-like patches that appear for a few days or weeks, disappear completely, and then return after a period of time, it often suggests a recurring inflammatory skin condition rather than simply having chronically dry skin.  This pattern is actually quite common with eczema, particularly atopic dermatitis and contact dermatitis.  The fact that the spots disappear on their own doesn't necessarily mean the underlying tendency has gone away. Eczema is often cyclical: your skin barrier becomes irritated, inflammation develops, the skin heals, and then something triggers another flare.  What could be causing it? There are a few possibilities:  1. Atopic dermatitis (classic eczema)  Dry, rough, sometimes slightly red or discolored patches.  Can be itchy, although not always intensely.  Flares can last days or weeks before settling down.  Can be triggered by cold weather, stress, sweating, hot showers, or changes in skincare.  2. Contact dermatitis  Happens when your skin reacts to something it comes into contact with.  Common triggers include fragrances, laundry detergent, body wash, skincare products, metals, and certain fabrics.  Can appear intermittently depending on when you're exposed to the irritant or allergen.  Often appears in specific areas of the body.  3. Nummular eczema  Produces dry, sometimes itchy, coin-shaped patches.  Individual patches can persist for weeks and then resolve.  Often appears on the arms, legs, and torso.  4. Psoriasis or another skin condition  Sometimes mistaken for eczema.  Psoriasis tends to produce more clearly defined, thicker patches with scaling.  A fungal rash can also resemble eczema, particularly when it forms circular patches.  Why does it disappear and come back? This is actually one of the most useful clues.  For example:  If the patches appear in the same locations repeatedly, it could indicate recurring eczema or an ongoing contact allergy.  If they appear in different locations, environmental triggers or atopic dermatitis may be more likely.  If they appear during certain seasons, weather and humidity could be contributing.  If they appear after introducing new skincare, detergent, clothing, or jewelry, contact dermatitis becomes a stronger possibility.  The American Academy of Dermatology specifically notes that contact dermatitis can come and go when exposure to an allergen is intermittent. convo_text: My eye doctor is sending me to a retina specialist, the appt is supposed to take 3-4 hours what will they do A 3–4 hour first visit with a retina specialist is fairly common. It usually doesn't mean they're expecting to do a procedure that day. Retina clinics often do a very thorough evaluation, and some of the testing takes time.  You can expect something like this:  Detailed vision and eye examination  They'll check each eye's vision, pupils, eye pressure, and peripheral vision. The doctor will examine the retina and optic nerve carefully. Dilating your pupils  They'll put drops in your eyes to get a much better view of the retina. Your vision may be blurry and light-sensitive for several hours afterward, so bringing sunglasses is a good idea. If your vision is significantly impaired afterward, having someone drive you is wise. Retinal photographs  They may take high-resolution photographs of the back of your eye to document what they see. OCT scan  This is very common. You simply look into a machine while it takes detailed cross-sectional pictures of the retina. It can show things that aren't visible during a normal eye exam, such as retinal swelling, fluid, thinning, or changes in the macula. Possibly a fluorescein angiogram  Depending on what your eye doctor saw, they may inject a fluorescent dye into a vein in your arm and take a series of pictures as the dye travels through the blood vessels in your retina. Not everyone needs this test. Possibly an ultrasound or other specialized imaging  This is more likely if they need to look behind or through something that makes the retina difficult to see. Consultation with the retina doctor  They'll review the tests and explain what they see. They may tell you that they simply want to monitor it, recommend treatment, or schedule another visit/procedure. Why 3–4 hours?
